title: The bow in the clouds (Genesis 8–9)
hookLine: after the flood, God's promise with every living thing

lines: A DOVE WITH AN OLIVE LEAF.
cards: A hundred and fifty days, the water rules the earth. Then it begins to fall. The ark grounds on the mountains of Ararat.
Noah opens the window and sends out a raven, which flies back and forth. Then a dove, which finds nowhere to land and comes back to his hand.
He waits seven days and sends her again, and at evening she returns with an olive leaf in her beak. Seven days more, and she doesn't come back at all.
A dove with an olive branch still turns up on flags and posters as a sign of peace. But the story isn't finished when the ground dries.

teach.b: First, the word. Covenant, in Hebrew berit, is a binding promise between two parties, more than a contract, closer to a family bond. God promised one to Noah before the flood; here it is made.

teach.h: EVERY LIVING CREATURE IS IN IT.
teach.b: Second, who's in it: Noah, his sons, their children after them, and, the text keeps saying, every living creature, birds, cattle, beasts of the earth. The animals are partners in a promise.
Third, what's promised: never again will a flood destroy the earth.

teach.h: A BOW HUNG IN THE CLOUDS.
teach.b: And the sign, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me, and between the earth." The Hebrew word for bow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a warrior's bow.

Some readers picture God hanging up the weapon, pointed away from the earth; the text doesn't spell that out. But the text is clear about who the sign is for: when the bow appears, God says, I will remember.
Fourth, why the Church cares. The Catechism places this covenant within God's plan of salvation, and says it stays in force for the nations until the gospel is proclaimed to the whole world.
It closes a week that began with a lonely man in a garden: a serpent's question, a call into the trees, the first good news, a brother's blood, an ark, and now color across the sky.

how: The Church reads God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:8–15) on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, and the Catechism describes it as God's covenant with all the nations.

o: a binding promise, closer to a family bond
a rainbow sent to show a storm is over
a written contract signed by two kings

games.q: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.

s: God's covenant after the flood is with Noah alone
it's with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature that came out of the ark.
in the story, the rainbow reminds God
when the bow appears, God says, I will remember.
the raven brings back the olive leaf
the raven flies back and forth. the dove returns with an olive leaf on her second flight.

games.q: the waters have gone down and every creature is out of the ark. God speaks to Noah. what sign does God give?
o: a new altar built on Ararat.
a bow set in the clouds.
the dove that never came back.
games.why: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant." and the reminder, the text says, is for God.

practice: If you can see a window, look out of it now; if not, picture the last sky you noticed, and let your eyes rest on whatever color is there.

Then think of every creature under that same sky, birds, a neighbor's dog, a fish you'll never see, a stranger across the world, all inside one promise in the story. If you pray, give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Covenant. Berit in Hebrew: a binding promise. After the flood, God makes one with Noah and every living creature, and sets a bow in the clouds as its sign.

orig.note: Hebrew: covenant, a binding promise. promised to Noah in Genesis 6 and made in chapter 9.

carryVoice: Your line: a promise to every creature. The birds and the beasts are in it too. That's the week.
